title: Ezra
subtitle: The return from exile and the rebuilt Temple
lead: Ezra tells how the Jews came home from exile in Babylon and rebuilt their life around the house of God in Jerusalem. It opens where 2 Chronicles ends, with the Persian king Cyrus telling God's people to go up and build the LORD's house again. A first group returns, sets up the altar and lays the foundation of the Temple. Then opposition stops the work for years, until the prophets Haggai and Zechariah stir the people and King Darius orders the building finished.

The second half jumps about sixty years, to Ezra himself, a priest and scribe sent by King Artaxerxes to teach God's law in Judah. Ezra leads a second return, and when he learns that many men have married women from the peoples around them, he prays a long prayer of confession and the people agree to send the wives away. The book quotes Persian royal letters in their own language, Aramaic, and Ezra's own memoir in the first person.
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 15a): Ezra wrote his own book, and Nehemiah finished it. Most scholars see an unnamed editor who used Ezra's first-person memoir (7:27–9:15), lists and an Aramaic file of letters. Most scholars now think a different hand from Chronicles; some still argue for a common author or school.

Written after the events: most scholars say about 400–300 BC, a few as early as about 440 BC. The story runs from Cyrus's decree (538 BC) to the Temple's completion (515 BC), then from Ezra's journey (usually dated 458 BC) to the marriage inquiry of the next year.
Babylon, the Persian court and Jerusalem, in the small Persian province of Judah (Yehud), part of the province "Beyond the River" west of the Euphrates.

Historical narrative built around documents: a royal decree (1:2–4), lists of people and Temple vessels (1:9–11; 2; 8; 10:18–44), official Aramaic letters (4:11–22; 5:7–17; 6:3–12; 7:12–26), Ezra's memoir and a prayer of confession (9:6–15).
Hebrew, with two long passages in Aramaic, the official language of the Persian empire (4:8–6:18; 7:12–26).

10 chapters, 280 verses. In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, called Ezra; the Masoretes counted their verses together. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) puts Ezra just before Chronicles at the end of the Bible, and most printed Hebrew Bibles, like the Talmud, end with Chronicles; the Aleppo and Leningrad codices put Chronicles first among the Writings and Ezra–Nehemiah last, so the Bible ends with Nehemiah. Christian Bibles place it after Chronicles.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: Ezra is a true account of the return from Babylon, written largely by Ezra himself (Bava Batra 15a), with copies of Persian royal letters and Ezra's own memoir in the first person (7:27–9:15). Ezra and Nehemiah were counted as one book in the Hebrew Bible.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars date the finished book to the late Persian or early Greek period and see an editor combining lists, an Aramaic file of letters (4:8–6:18; 7:12–26) and Ezra's memoir. They debate whether the letters are genuine Persian documents, how the book's order of events fits the Persian kings, and whether Ezra came before or after Nehemiah.

lenses.name: Persian records
lenses.desc: Ezra is the Bible's richest window on Persian rule: royal decrees, letters between governors and the court, archives searched at Ecbatana (6:2), and officials like Tattenai, who appears in a Babylonian tablet. The Cyrus Cylinder, the Elephantine papyri and the Persepolis tablets let readers test its picture of the empire.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis call Ezra a second Moses: 'Ezra was worthy that the Torah be given through him, had Moses not come before him' (Sanhedrin 21b). Tradition credits him and the Men of the Great Assembly with the square Hebrew script, public Torah reading and the shaping of the Scriptures.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Christians read the return and the rebuilt Temple as part of God keeping his promises through the exile, leading to the second Temple where Jesus taught. The book's demand that men send away foreign wives (9–10) has long troubled Christian readers, who set it beside Ruth and the welcome of the nations.

audience.to: The Jewish community of the small Persian province of Judah (Yehud) and its Temple in Jerusalem, probably some generations after Ezra and Nehemiah, in the late Persian or early Greek period (about 400–300 BC). They were a minority in their own land, ruled by a foreign empire, worshiping in a Temple far plainer than Solomon's, and divided from their neighbors over who belonged to Israel.
audience.why: To show them that their community stood in unbroken line with the Israel of Moses and David: God had moved Persian kings to send them home, the house had been rebuilt by royal permission, against opposition and through his prophets, and the law of Moses had been taught and accepted. Knowing this audience explains the book's lists of families and clergy (who belongs), its copies of royal letters (our right to be here), its stress on doing things 'as it is written,' and its hard line on separation, which answered real questions about identity in a mixed land.
views: Traditional readers, following the Talmud, hold that Ezra himself wrote the book (with Nehemiah finishing it) for the community of his own day, about 440–400 BC, to record how God restored them and to call them to keep the law.

Most critical scholars think an editor about 400–300 BC combined Ezra's memoir, Nehemiah's memoir, lists and Aramaic documents to give a later community its founding story, and some see the book as taking a side in disputes with Samaria and with Judeans who had never been exiled.

Those who hold that the Chronicler also wrote Ezra–Nehemiah read the books together as one history from Adam to Nehemiah, written for Temple circles in Jerusalem; most scholars since Japhet and Williamson read them as separate works with different emphases.

authorship: The Talmud says "Ezra wrote his book and the genealogy of Chronicles up to his own time," and that Nehemiah finished it (Bavli Bava Batra 15a). On this view Ezra, the priest and scribe who came to Jerusalem in Artaxerxes' seventh year (7:7–8), wrote the book from his own memoir and from the documents he quotes, and Ezra and Nehemiah were one book. The first-person sections (7:27–9:15) and the royal letters, kept in their Aramaic, fit a writer close to the events.
Critical scholarship: an editor using sources

Most scholars think an unnamed editor composed Ezra–Nehemiah about 400–300 BC from several sources: Ezra's memoir, Nehemiah's memoir, lists (Ezra 2; 8; 10; Nehemiah 7; 10–12) and an Aramaic collection of letters (4:8–6:18; 7:12–26). The high-priestly line in Nehemiah 12:10–11, 22 runs to Jaddua, which many place late in the Persian period. Williamson argues that chapters 1–6 were written last, as an introduction built from the documents.

Since Leopold Zunz (1832), many held that one "Chronicler" wrote Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah as one history (Curtis and Madsen; Martin Noth). The shared ending and beginning (2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–3) and the interest in Levites, singers and Temple worship seemed to prove it. Sara Japhet (1968) and H. G. M. Williamson (1977) compared their language and ideas and concluded they are separate works, and most scholars now agree, though some, such as Blenkinsopp, still argue for a common author or school. 1 Esdras, which runs straight from Chronicles into Ezra, has been cited on both sides.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew and Aramaic, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Key terms match the rest of the site: YHWH is "the LORD"; hesed is "loyal love" (3:11); netinim are "the temple servants" (2:43); bene haggolah are "the people of the exile" (4:1; 6:19); torah is "law" (3:2); the province west of the Euphrates is "Beyond the River" (4:10).

Aramaic

Ezra 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26 are in Aramaic, the official language of the Persian empire. The Plain translates the official letters as letters, keeping their formulas: the address, the greeting "Peace," the turn to business with "And now," "Let the king know," and closing orders. The chapter pages mark where the Aramaic begins and ends.

Parallel passages

Ezra 1:1–3 repeats 2 Chronicles 36:22–23. Where the Hebrew is the same, the Plain uses the site's wording of 2 Chronicles exactly; where it differs ("from Jeremiah's mouth," "May his God be with him," and the longer ending), the English differs too. Ezra 2 is nearly the same list as Nehemiah 7:6–73; the notes and the chapter page give the differences.

The text and the Greek

The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex. Where the Masoretes mark a reading to be read aloud (Qere) in place of the written text (Ketiv), the Plain follows the Qere, with two exceptions: 4:9, where the written "that is" makes better sense than the Qere's unknown "Dehavites," and 4:11, where both mean the same. The variants list every pair that changes a name or the English (2:46; 2:50; 3:3; 4:2; 4:7; 4:9; 4:11). The other pairs in chapters 1–6 are spelling only. The Plain departs from the Leningrad Codex itself only at 2:25 (Kiriath-jearim), where a variant explains why. The Greek comes in two forms. 2 Esdras (Esdras B) is a close translation of Ezra–Nehemiah; where this site cites it, the reading was checked in Rahlfs' edition. 1 Esdras (Esdras A) is a freer parallel, with a different order of events and the story of the three guards; it is cited from the KJV Apocrypha and the commentaries, in KJV verse numbers, which differ in places from Rahlfs' numbering (Cyrus's list of vessels, for example, is 2:13–14 in the KJV and 2:9–11 in Rahlfs).

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

The book has two halves about sixty years apart. Chapters 1–6 cover 538–515 BC: Cyrus's decree, the return, the altar and foundation, the opposition, the prophets, and the finished Temple. They are told in the third person and built around documents. Chapters 7–10 jump to Artaxerxes' seventh year (usually 458 BC): Ezra's journey with a royal letter, his memoir in the first person (7:27–9:15), and the crisis over mixed marriages. Both halves follow a similar pattern: a Persian king's decree, a journey, gifts for the Temple, and a challenge to the community's identity. Chapter 4 breaks time order on purpose, gathering opposition from Xerxes and Artaxerxes into the story of the Temple.

In the Hebrew Bible Ezra and Nehemiah were one book, called Ezra. The Talmud treats them so (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a), and the Masoretes counted their verses together, placing the middle of the book at Nehemiah 3:32. Origen and Jerome knew the division into two, and Jerome's Latin Bible called them 1 and 2 Esdras; Hebrew Bibles adopted the division only in the late Middle Ages. In the Talmud's order the book comes just before Chronicles at the end of the Writings. In the Aleppo and Leningrad codices, which this site follows, Chronicles comes first among the Writings and Ezra–Nehemiah last, so the Bible ends with Nehemiah. Christian Bibles, following the Greek, place it after Chronicles among the histories.

The Persian kings in Ezra are Cyrus (king of Babylon 539–530 BC), Darius I (522–486), Ahasuerus, that is Xerxes I (486–465), and Artaxerxes I (465–424). The return under Cyrus is usually dated 538 BC, the Temple's completion 515 BC (6:15), and Ezra's arrival 458 BC (7:7–8). A long debate concerns whether Ezra came before or after Nehemiah (who came in 445 BC). The traditional order, with Ezra first in 458, is held by many scholars, including Williamson. Some put Ezra in the seventh year of Artaxerxes II, 398 BC, after Nehemiah, because Nehemiah's lists rarely mention Ezra and Ezra seems to find Jerusalem already inhabited and walled. Others emend 7:7 to the thirty-seventh year (428 BC). The book itself presents the two men as working together (Nehemiah 8:9; Nehemiah 12:26, 36).

Ezra keeps asking who belongs. It counts families and checks priests' records (2), refuses help from the people of the land (4:3), welcomes those who separate themselves to seek the LORD (6:21), and ends with men sending away foreign wives (9–10). Traditional readers see faithfulness: a small community protecting its worship from the idolatry that led to exile (9:1–2, 10–14). Many modern readers, Jewish and Christian, are troubled, especially by the divorces and their effect on women and children, and set the book beside Ruth, Isaiah 56:3–7 and Jonah, which welcome foreigners. Historians note that the conflict was also about land, power and identity in a small province. The site presents each reading and lets the text speak for itself.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians read Ezra
sections.b:
In Jewish tradition Ezra is a second Moses: "Ezra was worthy that the Torah be given through him, had Moses not come before him" (Bavli Sanhedrin 21b). The rabbis credit him and the Men of the Great Assembly with the square Hebrew script, public reading of the Torah on market days and Sabbaths, and the shaping of the Scriptures; the founding of the second Temple begins the Second Temple period of Jewish history. The dedication of 6:16 shares its name, chanukkah, with the later feast of Hanukkah.

Christians read Ezra as part of God keeping his promises through the exile, so that the Messiah would come to a people in the land and teach in this rebuilt Temple. Jesus' genealogies run through Zerubbabel (Matthew 1:12–13; Luke 3:27). Christian preachers have long used the rebuilding of the Temple as a picture of the church's renewal, and Ezra's devotion to the law (7:10) as a model of the teacher's life. The book's demand for divorce in chapters 9–10 has always needed careful reading in light of 1 Corinthians 7:12–14.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a book about permission
spec.body: My own reading: Ezra is a book about permission. Every step of the restoration needs two permissions, one from God and one from the king. God rouses Cyrus and the king decrees (1:1–4); the prophets speak and Darius confirms (5:1–6:12); "the good hand of his God" is on Ezra and Artaxerxes grants all he asks (7:6). When the people move without both, as when they rebuild walls without royal leave (4:12–23), the work stops. The book teaches a people living under empire that faithfulness and lawful submission can work together, and that the God of the heavens rules the king's heart (6:22). Many scholars stress the book's documents and its positive view of Persia (Eskenazi; Williamson; Blenkinsopp); naming the double permission as the book's organizing idea is my own suggestion.

prompts:
In a Persian treasury hall with fluted stone columns and bull-headed capitals, a Persian treasurer in a tall fluted hat and long pleated robe counts gold and silver basins and bowls laid out in rows on reed mats. A scribe with a pen case writes on a leather scroll. Facing them stands a Judean leader in a simple robe and head cloth, hands open to receive. Behind him, through an open doorway, a caravan of donkeys and families waits in the morning light.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Weeping and shouting at the foundation (3:10–13)

On a rocky hilltop among ruined walls, a line of fresh foundation stones is laid. Priests in white linen raise long silver trumpets; Levites clash bronze cymbals. A crowd of young men and women shout with raised arms, while a group of old, white-bearded men stands apart, covering their faces and weeping. Sound lines ripple outward from the crowd across the hills.

The standard detailed commentary, careful on the sources, the Aramaic documents and the history.
A critical commentary attentive to the book's social conflicts and its picture of the community.

traditions.q: Is 1 Esdras, the Greek retelling of the end of 2 Chronicles, Ezra and part of Nehemiah 8, part of the Old Testament?
views: Yes, for the Greek church. Greek Orthodox Bibles print it as the first book of Esdras, before Ezra–Nehemiah, and read it with the rest of the Old Testament. Other Orthodox churches number it differently, and no council has fixed its place for all of them.
No. The Council of Trent's list of 1546 left it out. The official Latin Bible of 1592 printed it, as 3 Esdras, in an appendix after the New Testament, so that it would not be lost.

Article 6 lists it, as the Third Book of Esdras, among the books the church reads for example of life and instruction in manners, but not to establish any doctrine. The King James Version printed it first among the Apocrypha.
Luther left it out of his Bible altogether, with 4 Ezra. In his preface to Baruch he said these two books held nothing that could not be found better in Aesop.

No. It belongs to the Apocrypha, which the Westminster Confession says is not inspired and has no more authority in the church than other human writings (1.3). Reformed readers use it only as an early witness to the history and the text.
